title: What to read for the exam: 24 topics and their required reading

1.title: How the exam is built
1.text: This document is the official schedule of the module examination in EUROPEAN AND GLOBAL LEGAL HISTORY, and it is worth knowing because it tells you exactly what is expected of you. THE EXAM HAS TWENTY-FOUR TOPICS and EACH ONE HAS REQUIRED READING ASSIGNED TO IT — either paragraphs from OLECHOWSKI'S TEXTBOOK 'INTRODUCTION TO AUSTRIAN AND EUROPEAN LEGAL HISTORY' (2nd edition, 2025), or a separate scholarly text, or both. The structure of the list reveals two things. FIRST: THE CENTRE OF GRAVITY IS THE TEXTBOOK; separate texts are assigned to only nine topics — so anyone who reads only the articles and skips the textbook misses most of the material. SECOND: SOME TOPICS SHARE THE SAME TEXT, which suggests they are examined in pairs — topics 9 to 11 share Sunde's Comparing Legal Cultures, topics 16 and 17 the same block of Olechowski, topics 18 and 19 both Stolleis and Kress, and topics 23 and 24 Kennedy. Whoever studies in pairs studies the way the list is built.

cards.q: Which topics share the same required text, and what follows from that?

4.title: Topics 1 to 8 and their reading
4.text: 1. INTRODUCTION: METHODS, SOURCES, AIMS OF LEGAL HISTORY — Olechowski, paras 0001–0006. 2. ANCIENT LEGAL CULTURES; HISTORY OF ISLAMIC LAW — JOHANSEN, WEISS, MOTZKI, entry 'Islamic Law' in the Oxford International Encyclopedia of Legal History (2009), plus Olechowski paras 1001–1306, 2101–2102, 2301–2304. 3. THE DEVELOPMENT OF LAW IN THE MIDDLE AGES — Olechowski, paras 2103–2114, 2201–2219, 2221–2223, 2305–2314, 2316–2321. 4. IUS COMMUNE AND THE EARLY MODERN PERIOD — Olechowski, paras 2115–2119, 2225, 2322–2327. 5. JEWISH LEGAL HISTORY — BEN-MENAHEM, entry 'Jewish Law' in the International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (2001), plus paras 1302, 2224, 2315, 2331. 6. COMMON LAW — HERZOG, A Short History of European Law (2018), ch. 6, plus paras 2328–2330. 7. THE WESTPHALIAN ORDER AND EARLY CONSTITUTIONALISM — DUCHHARDT, From the Peace of Westphalia to the Congress of Vienna, in: Fassbender, Peters (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of the History of International Law (2012), pp. 628–653, plus paras 3101–3108, 3201–3206, 3208–3209. 8. NATURAL LAW, ENLIGHTENMENT AND REVOLUTION — IBBETSON, Natural Law in Early Modern Legal Thought, in: Pihlajamäki, Dubber, Godfrey (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of European Legal History (2018), pp. 566–582, plus paras 3109–3123, 3207, 3210–3211, 3301–3303.

cards.q: Which required reading belongs to topics 2, 5 and 6?
cards.a: TOPIC 2 (ancient cultures and Islamic law): JOHANSEN, WEISS, MOTZKI, entry 'Islamic Law' in the Oxford International Encyclopedia of Legal History (2009). TOPIC 5 (Jewish legal history): BEN-MENAHEM, entry 'Jewish Law' in the International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (2001). TOPIC 6 (common law): HERZOG, A Short History of European Law (2018), ch. 6.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: Which required reading belongs to topics 7 and 8?
cards.a: TOPIC 7 (the Westphalian order and early constitutionalism): DUCHHARDT, From the Peace of Westphalia to the Congress of Vienna, in The Oxford Handbook of the History of International Law (2012), pp. 628–653. TOPIC 8 (natural law, Enlightenment, revolution): IBBETSON, Natural Law in Early Modern Legal Thought, in The Oxford Handbook of European Legal History (2018), pp. 566–582.

6.title: Topics 9 to 15 and their reading
6.text: 9., 10. AND 11. CONSTITUTIONALISM AND NORM PRODUCTION I, II, III — jointly: KOCH, SKODVIN, SUNDE (eds.), COMPARING LEGAL CULTURES, 2nd ed. 2017 — INTRODUCTION, CHAPTER 10 (ENGLAND AND WALES), CHAPTER 13 (FRANCE), CHAPTER 14 (AUSTRIA); for parts I–III, Olechowski paras 2220, 3304–3315, 4101–4117, 4201–4227, 4301–4312, 6301–6302. Note which three countries the handbook picked — they are exactly the three on which Foljanty's exercise class demonstrates the three models of norm production. 12. LEGAL EDUCATION AND THE LEGAL PROFESSIONS — Olechowski, paras 3316, 4306, 8305. (Only three paragraphs, the smallest topic in the whole exam.) 13. IMPERIALISM AND CONSTITUTIONALISM BEFORE 1914 — WENZLHUEMER, entry 'Colonial Systems of Law (British Empire)', and GUÉRAICHE, entry 'Colonial Systems of Law (French Empire)', both in the Encyclopedia of Western Colonialism since 1450 (2007), pp. 709–711 and 713–714, plus paras 4118–4125. 14. CHINESE LEGAL HISTORY — XU, Heaven has Eyes: Law and Justice in Chinese History (2020), pp. 7–39, and CHEN, Traditionalising Chinese Law, in: Zhao/Ng (eds.), Chinese Legal Reform and the Global Legal Order (2017), pp. 181–210. 15. THE FIRST WORLD WAR AND THE PARIS PEACE CONFERENCE — GASSNER, From Brest-Litovsk via St. Germain to Sèvres, Journal on European History of Law 1/2023, pp. 2–14, plus paras 4126, 6101–6105.

cards.q: What is the required reading for topics 9–11, and what does the choice of chapters reveal?
cards.a: KOCH, SKODVIN, SUNDE (eds.), COMPARING LEGAL CULTURES (2nd ed. 2017): the INTRODUCTION, CHAPTER 10 (England and Wales), CHAPTER 13 (France), CHAPTER 14 (Austria). The choice reveals that these are exactly THE THREE COUNTRIES ON WHICH FOLJANTY'S EXERCISE CLASS DEMONSTRATES THE THREE MODELS OF NORM PRODUCTION.

cards.q: Which reading belongs to topics 13, 14 and 15?
cards.a: TOPIC 13 (imperialism): WENZLHUEMER, 'Colonial Systems of Law (British Empire)' and GUÉRAICHE, 'Colonial Systems of Law (French Empire)', both in the Encyclopedia of Western Colonialism since 1450 (2007). TOPIC 14 (Chinese legal history): XU, Heaven has Eyes (2020), pp. 7–39, and CHEN, Traditionalising Chinese Law (2017), pp. 181–210. TOPIC 15 (the First World War): GASSNER, From Brest-Litovsk via St. Germain to Sèvres (2023).

9.title: Topics 16 to 24 and their reading
9.text: 16. AND 17. THE AUSTRIAN FIRST REPUBLIC, DEMOCRACY AND THE B-VG I AND II — jointly Olechowski, paras 6106–6119, 6201–6226, 6303–6305, 8201–8203. 18. AND 19. DICTATORSHIPS OF THE 20TH CENTURY I AND II — jointly STOLLEIS, European Twentieth-Century Dictatorship and the Law, in: Pihlajamäki, Dubber, Godfrey (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of European Legal History (2018), and KRESS, entry 'International Criminal Law' in the Max Planck Encyclopedia of Public International Law (2009), plus paras 4313–4316, 5101–5301, 7101–7113, 7201–7219, 7301–7303. (Note the span of paragraphs: this is by far the largest block of the textbook in the whole exam.) 20. EUROPE DURING THE COLD WAR (1945–1955) — Olechowski, paras 8104, 8106–8115, 8204–8208. 21. EUROPE AND EUROPEAN INTEGRATION SINCE 1955 — Olechowski, paras 8116–8122, 8124–8147, 8209–8221. 22. HER STORY — Olechowski, paras 3212, 4226, 6226. (Three paragraphs, the same small span as topic 12 — and yet it is a topic of its own.) 23. AND 24. GLOBALISATION OF LAW I AND II — jointly DUNCAN KENNEDY, Three Globalizations of Law and Legal Thought: 1850–2000, in: Trubek, Santos (eds.), The New Law and Economic Development (2006), pp. 19–73, plus paras 8101–8103, 8105, 8123, 8222–8224, 8301–8304.

cards.q: Which reading belongs to topics 18 and 19, and what is special about that block?
cards.a: STOLLEIS, European Twentieth-Century Dictatorship and the Law (The Oxford Handbook of European Legal History, 2018) and KRESS, entry 'International Criminal Law' in the Max Planck Encyclopedia of Public International Law (2009). What is special is the SPAN OF TEXTBOOK PARAGRAPHS (4313–4316, 5101–5301, 7101–7113, 7201–7219, 7301–7303) — BY FAR THE LARGEST BLOCK in the whole exam.

cards.q: Which topics have the smallest amount of required reading?
cards.a: TOPIC 12 (legal education and the professions) — only paras 3316, 4306, 8305 — and TOPIC 22 (HER STORY) — paras 3212, 4226, 6226. THREE PARAGRAPHS each, and yet both are exam topics in their own right.

cards.q: What is the required reading for topics 23 and 24?
cards.a: DUNCAN KENNEDY, Three Globalizations of Law and Legal Thought: 1850–2000, in: Trubek, Santos (eds.), The New Law and Economic Development (2006), pp. 19–73 — plus Olechowski paras 8101–8103, 8105, 8123, 8222–8224, 8301–8304.
